methods.label: Subtract two right-triangle equations
methods.explanation:
Dropping perpendiculars from the shorter base creates two right triangles with the same height. Subtracting their Pythagorean equations will eliminate that height.

Up to reflection, take \(AD=10\) and \(BC=14\). Let \(E\) and \(F\) be the perpendicular feet from \(D\) and \(C\) to \(AB\). Because angles \(A\) and \(B\) are acute, these points lie in the order \(A,E,F,B\). The parallel bases give \(EF=CD=21\).

Set \(AE=p\), \(FB=q\), and let the common height be \(h>0\). Then
\[
p+q=33-21=12,
\]
and the two right triangles give
\[
p^2+h^2=100,\qquad q^2+h^2=196.
\]
Subtracting and factoring yields
\[
(q-p)(q+p)=96.
\]
Since \(p+q=12\), we obtain \(q-p=8\). Combining the sum and difference gives \(p=2\), \(q=10\), and hence
\[
h^2=100-2^2=96.
\]
The horizontal spans of diagonals \(AC\) and \(BD\) are respectively \(AF=2+21=23\) and \(BE=33-2=31\). They share the same height, so the diagonal with span \(23\) is shorter. Its length is
\[
\sqrt{23^2+96}=\sqrt{625}=\boxed{25},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{B}\). Exchanging the two legs reflects this configuration and leaves the two diagonal lengths unchanged.
